questions.q: Which list contains only vector quantities?
questions.solution: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Displacement, velocity and momentum all have a direction. Speed, mass, distance and energy are scalars: they have size only.

questions.q: A force of 20 N acts at 30° above the horizontal. What is its horizontal component?
questions.solution: The component next to the angle uses cosine: \(F_{x} = F\cos\theta = 20 \cos 30^{\circ}\) = 17 N. Using sine (10 N) finds the vertical component.

questions.q: Forces of 3.0 N and 4.0 N act on an object at right angles to each other. What is the magnitude of the resultant force?
questions.solution: Perpendicular vectors add by Pythagoras: \(F = \sqrt{3.0^{2} + 4.0^{2}} = \sqrt{25}\) = 5.0 N. Simply adding them (7.0 N) only works when they act in the same direction.

questions.q: A see-saw is balanced. A child of weight 300 N sits 1.2 m from the pivot. An adult sits 1.8 m from the pivot on the other side. What is the adult's weight?
questions.solution: In equilibrium the clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal. The child's moment is 300 × 1.2 = 360 N m. So the adult's weight is 360 ÷ 1.8 = 200 N.

questions.q: A uniform metre rule of weight 1.0 N is pivoted at its 40 cm mark. It balances horizontally when a load is hung from the 10 cm mark. What is the weight of the load?
questions.solution: The rule's weight acts at its centre of gravity, the 50 cm mark, which is 10 cm from the pivot. The load is 30 cm from the pivot on the other side. Taking moments about the pivot: W × 30 = 1.0 × 10, so W = 0.33 N.

questions.q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest at \(2.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}\) for 8.0 s. How far does it travel in this time?
questions.solution: \(s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}\) with \(u = 0\): \(s = \frac{1}{2} \times 2.5 \times 8.0^{2}\) = 80 m. Common slips are forgetting the half (160 m) or forgetting to square the time (10 m).

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at \(12\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Ignoring air resistance, what is the greatest height it reaches above the point of release? (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\))
questions.solution: At the top the velocity is zero. From \(v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as\) with \(a = -g\): \(h = \frac{u^{2}}{2g} = \frac{12^{2}}{2 \times 9.81}\) = 7.3 m. Leaving out the 2 (15 m) is the usual slip.

questions.q: What does the area under a velocity–time graph represent?
questions.solution: Area under a velocity–time graph is velocity multiplied by time, which is displacement. The gradient of the same graph is the acceleration.

questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at \(15\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) from the top of a cliff 20 m high. Ignoring air resistance, how far from the base of the cliff does it land? (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\))
questions.solution: Vertically it falls from rest: \(t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 20}{9.81}}\) = 2.02 s. Horizontally the velocity is constant: distance = 15 × 2.02 = 30 m.

questions.q: A projectile moves through the air with negligible air resistance. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Its horizontal velocity decreases steadily until it lands.
options.B: Its acceleration is zero at the highest point.
options.D: Its horizontal velocity is constant and its acceleration is always g downwards.

questions.solution: The only force is weight, which acts vertically. So there is no horizontal acceleration, and the vertical acceleration is g downwards throughout, including at the highest point, where only the vertical velocity is zero.

questions.q: A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 3000 N and a total resistive force of 600 N. What is its acceleration?
questions.solution: Use the resultant force: 3000 − 600 = 2400 N. Then \(a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{2400}{1200} = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}\). Using the driving force alone (2.5) ignores the resistive force.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. The Earth pulls the book down with a gravitational force. Which force is the Newton's third law pair of this force?

options.A: The gravitational force of the book pulling the Earth upwards.
options.B: The normal contact force of the table on the book.
options.C: The contact force of the book on the table.
options.D: The friction between the book and the table.

questions.solution: A third law pair is the same type of force, equal in size and opposite in direction, acting on two different objects. The Earth pulls the book, so the book pulls the Earth. The table's contact force also balances the weight, but it acts on the same object and is a different type of force.

questions.q: A skydiver is falling at terminal velocity. Which statement is correct?

options.A: There are no forces acting on her.
options.B: Her weight is greater than the drag force.
options.C: The drag force is greater than her weight.
options.D: The drag force equals her weight, so the resultant force is zero.

questions.solution: Drag grows with speed. At terminal velocity it has grown to equal the weight, so the resultant force is zero and, by Newton's first law, the velocity stays constant. Both forces still act.

questions.q: A trolley of mass 2.0 kg moving at \(3.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) collides with a stationary trolley of mass 4.0 kg. They stick together. What is their speed after the collision?
questions.solution: Momentum is conserved. Before: \(2.0 \times 3.0 = 6.0\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}\). After, the combined mass is 6.0 kg, so \(v = \frac{6.0}{6.0} = 1.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Dividing by 4.0 kg alone (1.5) forgets that both trolleys move.

questions.q: A constant force of 50 N acts for 0.20 s on a stationary ball of mass 0.40 kg. What is the speed of the ball afterwards?
questions.solution: Impulse equals change in momentum: \(F\Delta t = 50 \times 0.20 = 10\ \text{N s}\). The ball starts at rest, so \(v = \frac{10}{0.40} = 25\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

questions.q: Two objects collide inelastically, with no external forces acting. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not.
options.B: Kinetic energy is conserved, but momentum is not.
options.C: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
options.D: Neither momentum nor total energy is conserved.

questions.solution: Momentum is conserved in every collision with no external forces. In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy is transferred to other forms, such as heating, so kinetic energy falls. Total energy is still conserved.

questions.q: A force of 50 N pulls a sledge 4.0 m along level ground. The force acts at 60° to the direction of motion. How much work does the force do?
questions.solution: Only the component of the force along the motion does work: \(W = Fs\cos\theta = 50 \times 4.0 \times \cos 60^{\circ}\) = 100 J. Ignoring the angle (200 J) overstates it.

questions.q: The speed of a car doubles. What happens to its kinetic energy?

options.D: It increases by a factor of four.

questions.solution: \(E_{k} = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\), so kinetic energy depends on the speed squared. Doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by four. This is why braking distance rises so sharply with speed.

questions.q: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 5.0 m. Ignoring air resistance, what is its speed just before it hits the ground? (\(g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}\))
questions.solution: Gravitational potential energy lost equals kinetic energy gained: \(mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\). So \(v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.81 \times 5.0} = 9.9\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). The mass cancels, so it does not matter.

questions.q: An electric motor lifts a load of weight 200 N through 3.0 m in 4.0 s. The electrical power supplied to the motor is 250 W. What is the efficiency of the motor?
questions.solution: Useful work done: 200 × 3.0 = 600 J. Useful output power: 600 ÷ 4.0 = 150 W. Efficiency is useful output power divided by input power: 150 ÷ 250 = 0.60. An efficiency can never be more than 1.
